sections.text: Every reference points at a value that lives somewhere, and a reference must never outlive that value. The time a reference is valid is its lifetime. Most of the time Rust works lifetimes out by itself, and you have been relying on that all along. This lesson shows the cases where Rust asks for your help.
Here is a function that returns the longer of two string slices. It does not compile:

The result is a reference, but it borrows from either x or y, and Rust can't tell which. It needs to know how long the result stays valid. A lifetime annotation says it. A lifetime name is an apostrophe and a short name, usually 'a. You declare it in angle brackets, like a type parameter, then write it after the & of each reference:

Read it as: "x, y and the result all share the lifetime 'a. The result is valid only as long as both x and y are." The annotation does not make anything live longer. It only describes how the lifetimes of the inputs and the output relate, so the compiler can check every caller.
That check catches real bugs. Here result is used after second has been dropped at the end of the inner block. The compiler refuses:

Why did you never write lifetimes for functions like first_word(s: &str) -> &str? Rust fills them in using three elision rules. In plain words: (1) each reference parameter gets its own lifetime. (2) If there is exactly one input lifetime, the output gets it too. (3) If a method has &self or &mut self, the output gets the lifetime of self. When these rules leave the output unknown, as with longest (two inputs), you must write it yourself.
A struct that holds a reference needs a lifetime too, so Rust knows the struct can't outlive what it borrows:

Excerpt<'a> means "an Excerpt that borrows for 'a". It is declared after the name and used in the field. impl<'a> Excerpt<'a> repeats it, like impl<T> did for generics. first_word needs no annotation, because rule 3 applies. Because e borrows from novel, novel must stay alive as long as e is used.

There is one special lifetime, 'static. It means "valid for the whole run of the program". Every string literal has this type, &'static str, because the text is stored inside the program itself. Don't add 'static just to silence a compiler error. It usually hides a real problem.
If a lifetime error confuses you, ask: "who owns the data, and does the owner live long enough?" The owner is usually a String or Vec in some block. A reference to it can't outlive that block.

This is the check C and C++ leave to you (a returned pointer to a dead local is a dangling pointer). Garbage-collected languages avoid it by keeping objects alive. In Rust, lifetimes are erased after the check, so they cost nothing at run time. Labels like 'a only exist for the compiler.

exercise.prompt: longest is already written, and main already calls shorter. Add a function shorter that returns the shorter of two &str values (the first one if they are the same length). It should print two lines: forest and tree. Hint: shorter needs the same lifetime annotations as longest.

tests.label: Works when the shorter word comes second
The program prints forest, then tree
on a tie the first argument comes back
words a hard-coded tree would not match

hints: shorter has the same problem as longest: the result borrows from x or y, and Rust needs to be told how long it stays valid. Copy the shape of longest.
Give shorter the same lifetime annotations as longest: fn shorter<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str. In the body, change >= to <=, so a tie still gives x.
Return x when x.len() <= y.len(), otherwise y. The <= makes a tie give the first one. main already prints shorter("tree", "forest").

quiz.question: What does 'a in fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str tell the compiler?
options: The result lives for the whole program, whatever happens to x and y
The result stays valid only as long as both x and y do
x and y must have exactly the same length, so the result can be either one
quiz.explanation: The annotation 'a links the lifetimes: the returned reference is valid only while both x and y are valid, so the result can't outlive either. It doesn't make anything live forever, and x and y can have different lengths.

quiz.question: Why does fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str need no lifetime annotations?
options: Functions that return &str are exempt from lifetime checking
Because &str values are copied, so nothing can ever dangle
Elision rules: with exactly one input reference, the output gets its lifetime
quiz.explanation: Rust fills in lifetimes by itself with the elision rules. With exactly one input reference, the output reference gets that same lifetime, so you don't have to write it. Functions returning &str are not exempt, and a &str is not copied.

quiz.question: What is the type of a string literal like "hello"?
options: &'static str, valid for the whole run of the program
String, an owned value that is dropped at the end of its block
&'a str, valid only until the end of the nearest block
quiz.explanation: A string literal is stored inside the program itself, so it is valid for the whole run, which is the 'static lifetime. That makes its type &'static str. String is the owned type you create at run time with String::from.
